“Well, my dear, Mrs. Long says Netherfield has been rented by a wealthy young man from the north of England. He came on Monday in a carriage drawn by four horses to look at it, and liked it so much that he immediately reached an agreement with Mr. Morris. He will move in before Michaelmas, at the end of September, and some of his servants will arrive by the end of next week.”

“What is his name?”

“Bingley.”

“Is he married or single?”

“Oh, single, my dear, of course! A rich single man, with four or five thousand a year. How wonderful for our girls!”

“Why? What does it have to do with them?”

“My dear Mr. Bennet,” his wife replied, “why must you be so difficult? You know perfectly well I’m thinking of him marrying one of them.”

“Is that why he’s moving here?”

“Why? What nonsense! How can you say that? But he may very well fall in love with one of them, so you must visit him as soon as he arrives.”

“I don’t see any need. You and the girls can go. Or send them alone, which might be better still. Since you’re as pretty as any of them, Mr. Bingley might prefer you.”

“My dear, you flatter me. I certainly used to be quite beautiful, but I don’t claim to be anything special now. A woman with five grown daughters ought to stop thinking about her own looks.”

“In those circumstances, a woman seldom has much beauty left to think about.”

“But really, my dear, you must go and see Mr. Bingley when he moves into the neighborhood.”

“I certainly can’t promise that.”

“But think of your daughters. Imagine how comfortably one of them could live. Sir William and Lady Lucas have decided to visit him for that very reason, though you know they generally don’t call on newcomers. You really must go. We can’t visit him unless you do.”

“Surely you worry too much about the rules. I expect Mr. Bingley would be delighted to see you. I’ll send a short note with you, giving him my wholehearted permission to marry whichever daughter he chooses—though I must put in a good word for my little Lizzy.”

“You must do nothing of the kind. Lizzy is no better than the others. She certainly isn’t half as beautiful as Jane or half as cheerful as Lydia.”

“Why, that suggestion could give us quite a thrilling superstition. I suppose you’ll name the beetle scarabæus caput hominis, or something similar; natural history books are full of names like that. But where are those antennae you mentioned?”

“The antennae!” said Legrand, growing inexplicably heated. “Surely you can see the antennae. I drew them as clearly as they appear on the actual insect, which I should think is enough.”

“All right,” I said, “perhaps you did, but I still can’t see them.” I handed back the paper without further comment, unwilling to upset him. Yet I was very surprised by this turn of events. His irritation baffled me, and there were certainly no antennae visible in the beetle drawing, which really did look remarkably like an ordinary illustration of a skull.

He took the paper crossly and seemed about to crumple it and toss it into the fire, when a passing glance at the drawing suddenly arrested his attention. His face turned intensely red, then a moment later just as pale. For several minutes he remained seated, inspecting the drawing in close detail. Eventually he stood, took a candle from the table, and sat on a sea chest in the room’s farthest corner. There he examined the paper anxiously again, turning it every way. He said nothing. His behavior astonished me, but I thought it wiser to make no remark that might worsen his increasingly troubled mood. After a while he took a wallet from his coat pocket, carefully slipped the paper inside, and placed both in a writing desk, which he locked. His manner became calmer, although his earlier enthusiasm had entirely vanished. Still, he seemed distracted more than sulky. As the evening passed, he sank deeper into thought, and none of my attempts at lively conversation could bring him out of it. I had meant to spend the night at the hut, as I often had before, but seeing my host in this state, I felt it best to leave. He did not urge me to stay. As I departed, however, he shook my hand with even greater warmth than usual.

About a month later, during which I had seen nothing of Legrand, his servant Jupiter visited me in Charleston. I had never seen the good old Black man looking so dejected, and I feared that some serious misfortune had overtaken my friend.

“Each compares it, not to someone speaking a national language he knows, but to precisely the reverse. The Frenchman believes the voice belonged to a Spaniard, and says he ‘might have made out words had he known Spanish.’ The Dutchman insists it was a French voice; yet the report tells us that, ‘because he understood no French, the witness was questioned through an interpreter.’ The Englishman supposes the speaker German, although he ‘knows no German.’ The Spaniard ‘is certain’ it was an English voice, but bases his opinion entirely ‘on the intonation,’ since ‘he is unacquainted with English.’ The Italian takes it for a Russian voice, though he ‘has never spoken with a Russian native.’ Furthermore, another Frenchman contradicts the first, declaring positively that the voice was Italian; but as he does not know Italian, he too, like the Spaniard, ‘relies upon the intonation.’ How exceedingly strange that voice must have been to produce testimony of this description! Even its tones offered nothing recognizable to inhabitants of Europe’s five great divisions. You may suggest an Asiatic or an African speaker. Neither Asiatics nor Africans are numerous in Paris; without disputing your inference, however, I shall draw your attention to just three points. One witness describes the voice as ‘harsh rather than high-pitched.’ Two more characterize it as ‘rapid and uneven.’ Not one witness mentions distinguishing words, or even sounds that resembled words.

“I cannot tell,” Dupin went on, “what effect my reasoning has thus far had upon you. Nevertheless, I readily assert that sound deductions from this part of the evidence alone—the statements concerning the harsh and the shrill voices—suffice to create a suspicion that ought to guide every subsequent stage of the inquiry. I have said ‘sound deductions,’ but that does not quite convey my intention. I mean that these deductions are the only correct ones, and that this suspicion follows from them necessarily, as their sole outcome. I shall not yet disclose the suspicion itself. I ask you only to remember that it struck me powerfully enough to give my investigation of the room a particular shape and direction.

“Let us now imagine ourselves inside that chamber. What is the first thing we should look for? The route by which the murderers escaped. I think I may safely say that neither of us accepts supernatural occurrences.”
